Let’s talk about something that’s tough for a lot of us—honest confession and accountability, or as I like to say, breaking the power of secrecy.
You know, secrecy can be one of the most powerful forces that keeps people stuck in old patterns—especially when it comes to struggles with lust. When we keep things hidden, those struggles just seem to get stronger, don’t they? Shame and the fear of being judged can make it really hard to admit what’s going on, even to ourselves. But here’s the thing—real change has to start with honest confession. First, you’ve got to be honest with yourself. Then, open up to God, and, when you’re ready, to someone you trust.
Now, confession isn’t about beating yourself up or sinking into guilt. It’s really about dragging what’s been hidden out into the light, so you can finally see it for what it is—and start to deal with it. Picture a room that’s been closed off for years. Dust piles up, cobwebs everywhere. But the moment you open that door and sunlight pours in? That’s when real cleaning can start. Confession works the same way—it lets the light in and opens the door to healing.
The next step is accountability. And let’s be clear: this isn’t about putting yourself under a microscope or inviting people to judge you. It’s about asking others to come alongside you—as companions. Trusted friends, a mentor, maybe someone from your faith community—they can be a source of support, encouragement, and even a gentle challenge when you need it. The goal isn’t surveillance. It’s about building relationships where you can be honest, and where real growth can actually happen.
So, how do you make accountability work in real life? Well, here are a few practical steps:
First, find one or two people you can really trust—folks who’ll listen without judging, and who can offer some wise advice.
Then, set up regular check-ins. Share what you’re struggling with, but don’t forget to celebrate the wins, too.
Agree on what you want to keep an eye on—whether that’s your media choices, your thought patterns, or certain situations that tend to trip you up.
And don’t underestimate the power of praying together, or just reminding each other that there’s always hope, and plenty of grace, for change.
Look, this whole process can feel pretty vulnerable—maybe even risky. But staying isolated only makes things harder. When you know you’re not alone, when you feel accepted even in your weak moments, shame starts to lose its grip.
And remember, accountability isn’t about being perfect. Everyone slips up sometimes. What matters is not keeping score of your failures, but building a habit of honesty and steady growth. Over time, confession and accountability become a kind of muscle memory—something that strengthens your resolve and makes real change possible.
